title: Tour de France stage 21: Pogacar confirms yellow as Van der Poel stuns in Paris. Was this best-ever final stage?
content:
Mathieu van der Poel pulled off one of the most astonishing victories of his career on Sunday, holding off the peloton on the Champs-Élysées to win stage 21 of the Tour de France.

Van der Poel and yellow jersey Tadej Pogačar worked together after going clear on the third and final ascent of the Montmartre climb, but it looked a long shot for them to hold off the various sprinters teams massed about 10 seconds behind them. Pogačar was caught with around 700 meters to go but Van der Poel pressed on, and found another surge of speed just as it looked like he was going to be overtaken.

Pogačar safely crossed the line in 30th place, and becomes a five-time winner of the Tour de France, one of only five men to ever reach that landmark, while Mads Pedersen, Richard Carapaz and Isaac del Toro win the green, polka dot and white jerseys respectively.

Jacob Whitehead and Duncan Alexander recap a memorable final stage of the 2026 race…

Van der Poel’s face was a grimace, Pogačar’s more of a smile, but both were rapt in pain. These were the expressions of men with nothing left to prove, but who put themselves there anyway.

Cycling’s beauty is in its unlikely alliances, the greatest classics rider of his generation and the greatest rider of any generation forged together on the Champs-Élysées, working together to find one of the lone prizes to have escaped them.

Van der Poel had attacked on the third climb of Montmartre, bringing only Pogačar with him. The pair time trialled their way to the line, bouncing over Parisian cobbles as they were chased down by a Visma-led group, then a Decathlon CMA CGM train, working for Olav Kooij.

This was an escape that should not have worked, a lead of just 12 seconds with 10km remaining. It showed the absurdity of these riders, of these performances, that it did.

Pogacar tied up, for the first time all Tour, in the final kilometer. He crossed the line at walking speed, a mortal for a moment at least, as much as the yellow jersey can be, freewheeling down the Champs-Élysées.

But out front, Van der Poel was still pushing, launching a heroic sprint with 800m to go. It was doomed until it wasn’t. Jasper Philipsen and Pedersen launched their sprints with 300m to go, Van der Poel’s legs visibly slowing in front of them. All three crossed the line in a blur. Philipsen’s arm went up. He celebrated his teammate’s win.

Van der Poel was near tears at the end, from exhaustion as much as anything else, using the barriers to help him stand.

His lifelong adversary Wout van Aert won here last year. It speaks to the greatness of their rivalry that Van der Poel emulated him today.

Pogačar paid tribute to Van der Poel’s win, saying “We both rode to the death, to the final. I ran out of gas. I knew we had to go out. He knew we had to go out. He took a beautiful victory today I think.”

Montmartre has again delivered a classic. In two years, it has produced the most memorable final stages of the Tour de France in decades, perhaps in race history. It has to stay.

Jacob Whitehead

One of the wonderful things about the Tour de France is how malleable the route is. New climbs, new roads and new challenges are found every year, and last year the organizers took inspiration from the 2024 Paris Olympics and added in the narrow, cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre — transforming the race’s final stage in the French capital into a puncheur’s dream, as evidenced by Van Aert’s solo victory in 2025.

And there was no hiding on the first of three times up Montmartre today, with Pedersen putting out monster watts to roar up the cobbled climb in front of huge crowds, followed by Pogačar, Van der Poel et al. But the organizers tweaked things from 2025, adding four kilometers between the end of the Montmartre and the finish line, to give the sprinters more of a chance. And the splinter group was duly caught before the next lap began — proof that the delicate balancing act was working as intended.

On the second ascent the selection was even more stellar, Pogačar and Van der Poel going clear of the entire peloton, joined a few moments later by Evenepoel and Pedersen. But once again, the peloton showed how collective power can reel in even the sport’s greatest engines.

But the third time was different. British champion Fred Wright was first to show his face on the climb, before Van der Poel and Pogačar went again. This time they got enough separation to build a lead of around 10 seconds. Not enough for most duos to hold off a hungry peloton, but this was two of the greatest riders the sport has ever seen. And we know what happened next.

The action today was some of the most exhilarating racing the Tour has witnessed for decades, and surely cements today’s format as the future of the final stage.

Duncan Alexander

It has been a bumper Tour for U.S. involvement. Just six riders, but each have played key roles in the race, particularly in now what appears to be the U.S.’ speciality — producing superdomestiques.

After missing out on selection last year, Brandon McNulty had an excellent Tour in support of Pogačar, particularly in pacing up the Tourmalet and Le Lioran. It was a shame that illness did not allow him to ride the final three stages with his team — though the Arizonan did bleach his hair in honor of team leader Pogacar.

Sepp Kuss and Matteo Jorgenson played similar roles on Visma, with Kuss in particular turning in another strong supporting performance, metronomic in the high mountains.

A stage win on Alpe d’Huez would have been merited, but given the circumstances of his second crash, it is a relief he avoided a potentially life-threatening incident.

Matthew Riccitello, best young rider at the Vuelta, also rode well as Paul Seixas’ last man. Expect to see him in this role for years to come.

Quinn Simmons helped deliver the green jersey to Pedersen, not always entirely willingly as he was forced to put his own ambitions to one side, but remains the best current rider to never stand on the Tour winner’s podium come day’s end.

Sean Quinn, meanwhile, was seconds from taking yellow on stage four after escaping on the road to Foix. Despite the lack of stage wins, this was a good Tour for American cycling.

For British cycling, however, results betrayed a little lack of depth. Tom Pidcock finished ninth on GC, but failed to get the stage win he craved — the first time in several years that the UK has had neither a stage win nor a top five on GC.

Oscar Onley was a major absence, but until Visma’s Matthew Brennan makes his Tour debut, the UK stands waiting for their next talent to come through.

Jacob Whitehead

In 2019, Julian Alaphilippe was within a couple of stages of winning the Tour de France — and bringing France’s drought to an end. Some believe he was even closer; a freak mudslide meaning times were taken from the top of the Col de l’Iseran, forcing him to cede yellow to Egan Bernal.

Alaphilippe’s performances were thrilling — the highlight an individual time trial win in Pau amongst possibly the most raucous atmosphere that the race has seen this century. A two-time World Champion, winner of six Tour stages and Milan-Sanremo, he is one of the modern greats.

This Tour was a goodbye lap of France, his legs finally out of power. “Don’t expect to see me again,” he said.

Other riders, too, are appearing in their final Tour. Uno-X’s Magnus Cort is retiring at the end of the season, so too Damiano Caruso (Bahrain Victorious), Luke Durbridge (Jayco-AlUla), Damien Howson (Pinarello Q36.5) and Ion Izagirre (Cofidis).

There will be more, too, who do not know they are making their last appearance in La Grand Boucle — it is this unknowingness which makes arriving in Paris special, whatever their situation.

Jacob Whitehead

Already, less than an hour after Van der Poel crossed the line, the barriers are coming down on the Champs-Élysées, the city’s yellow gilding returning to limestone. Following the Tour for three weeks, the manner in which the race appears and disappears is eerie, there is something both intangible and overwhelming about its presence.

Thanks so much for following the Tour on The Athletic throughout July — the fervor and interest has allowed us to cover it on the ground, chasing riders and stories over mountain passes, through boiling heat, and hundreds of kilometers of French motorways.

But Paris is only a finale of sorts. Next Saturday, the Tour de France Femmes begins in Switzerland — and for the first time, The Athletic will be following the race on every stage, through our colleague Jessica Hopkins.

We’ll have more stories from the men’s Tour over the coming days, but from Wednesday onwards… roll on the Femmes.
